label: thm:intro-all-points
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:intro-all-points}
For every $z\in\mathbb R$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-main}
   \inf_{b\in\mathcal F}F_z(b)
   =
   \log\Delta(S_a-z)+\frac12
   \qquad\text{in }[-\infty,\infty).
\end{equation}
Both sides equal $-\infty$ if and only if $z$ is an atom of $\mu_{S_a}$.
The regularized scales form a minimizing sequence:
$F_z(b_\varepsilon)\to\log\Delta(S_a-z)+\frac12$ as
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$.
head: environment
name: Variational formula at every real point

label: def:nondegenerate-regular
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:nondegenerate-regular}
A point $z\in\mathbb R$ is called \textbf{nondegenerate regular} if the
boundary value
$
   G(z+i0)
$
exists, and either
$
   -\operatorname{Im}G(z+i0)\succ0,
$
or $z$ belongs to an open component of
$
   \mathbb R\setminus\operatorname{supp}\mu_{S_a}.
$
head: environment
name: Nondegenerate regular point

label: thm:intro-attainment
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:intro-attainment}
Let $z$ be a nondegenerate regular point.  Then the regularized scales
converge, $b_z:=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}b_\varepsilon$ exists, and
the infimum in \eqref{eq:intro-main} is attained at $b_z$.  If $-\operatorname{Im}G(z+i0)\succ0$, then $b_z\in\partial\mathcal F$.
If $z$ lies in the resolvent set, then
$b_z\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal F$; if moreover $z$ lies in an
unbounded component of the resolvent set, then
$
   b_z=|G(z)|^{-1}.
$
head: environment
name: Attainment at nondegenerate regular points

label: thm:intro-capacity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:intro-capacity}
For $a=0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-capacity}
   \inf_{b\in\mathcal F}\Delta(b)
   =
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta)^{1/(2m)}.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\[
   \log\Delta(S_0)
   =
   -\frac12
   +
   \frac1{2m}\log\operatorname{Cap}(\eta),
\]
which is the Mai--Speicher formula.  Moreover, the infimum in
\eqref{eq:intro-capacity} is attained if and only if $\eta$ is
symmetrically doubly-stochastic scalable.
head: environment
name: Centered problem and capacity

label: cor:intro-brown
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:intro-brown}
Let $a_0,a_1,\dots,a_r\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ be arbitrary and
$S=a_0\otimes1+\sum_ia_i\otimes s_i$.  For $z\in\mathbb C$ let
$\mathcal F^{\mathrm h}\subset M_{2m}(\mathbb C)$ and
$F^{\mathrm h}_z$ be the feasible set and the functional
\eqref{eq:intro-F} of the self-adjoint matrix semicircle
\[
   H_z
   =
   \begin{pmatrix}0&S-z\\ S^*-\overline{z}&0\end{pmatrix}
   \in M_{2m}(\mathbb C)\otimes\mathcal A,
\]
at the spectral parameter $0$.  Then, for every $z\in\mathbb C$,
\[
   \log\Delta(S-z)
   =
   -\frac12+\inf_{b\in\mathcal F^{\mathrm h}}F^{\mathrm h}_z(b)
   \qquad\text{in }[-\infty,\infty),
\]
with both sides equal to $-\infty$ if and only if $S-z$ has a nontrivial
kernel, and with the infimum attained whenever $S-z$ is invertible.  In
particular, the Brown measure of $S$ is $\frac1{2\pi}\nabla_z^2$ of the
right-hand side.
head: environment
name: Brown measure of matrix-valued semicircular elements

label: thm:closed
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Closed determinant identity

title: Proof
body_md:
The key observation is that $H$ is a holomorphic primitive of the scalar
Cauchy transform.

Differentiate \eqref{eq:H-def}.  Since
\[
   \frac{d}{dw}\log\det G(w)
   =
   \operatorname{Tr}\bigl(G(w)^{-1}G'(w)\bigr),
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
   H'(w)
   &=
   -\operatorname{tr}_m\bigl(G^{-1}G'\bigr)
   \\
   &\quad
   +
   \frac12
   \operatorname{tr}_m\bigl(
      G'\eta(G)+G\eta(G')
   \bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
For the covariance map
\[
   \eta(X)=\sum_j A_jXA_j,
   \qquad A_j=A_j^*,
\]
cyclicity of the trace gives
\[
   \operatorname{tr}_m\bigl(G'\eta(G)\bigr)
   =
   \operatorname{tr}_m\bigl(G\eta(G')\bigr).
\]
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:H-prime-1}
   H'(w)
   =
   -\operatorname{tr}_m(G^{-1}G')
   +
   \operatorname{tr}_m\bigl(G\eta(G')\bigr).
\end{equation}

Differentiating the Dyson equation \eqref{eq:closed-dyson} gives
$
   -G^{-1}G'G^{-1}
   +
   \eta(G')
   =
   I,
$
and therefore
\[
   \eta(G')
   =
   I+G^{-1}G'G^{-1}.
\]
Substituting this into \eqref{eq:H-prime-1},
\begin{align*}
   \operatorname{tr}_m\bigl(G\eta(G')\bigr)
   &=
   \operatorname{tr}_mG
   +
   \operatorname{tr}_m(G'G^{-1}),
\end{align*}
so the logarithmic-derivative terms cancel and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:H-prime}
   \boxed{
   H'(w)=\operatorname{tr}_mG(w).
   }
\end{equation}

Now define the holomorphic logarithmic potential
\[
   \Lambda(w)
   :=
   \int_{\mathbb R}
   \log(w-t)\,d\mu_{S_a}(t),
   \qquad
   w\in\mathbb C^+,
\]
using the standard branch of the logarithm on the upper half-plane.
Then
\[
   \Lambda'(w)
   =
   \int_{\mathbb R}
   \frac{1}{w-t}\,d\mu_{S_a}(t)
   =
   \operatorname{tr}_mG(w).
\]
Thus
$
   H-\Lambda
$
is constant on $\mathbb C^+$.

As $|w|\to\infty$ non-tangentially,
\[
   G(w)
   =
   w^{-1}I+O(w^{-2}),
\]
and therefore
\[
   H(w)
   =
   \log w+o(1)
\]
up to the purely imaginary constant coming from the chosen branch of
$\log\det G$.  Similarly,
\[
   \Lambda(w)=\log w+o(1).
\]
Hence $H-\Lambda$ is purely imaginary, and consequently
\[
   \operatorname{Re}H(w)
   =
   \operatorname{Re}\Lambda(w)
   =
   \int_{\mathbb R}
   \log|w-t|\,d\mu_{S_a}(t).
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:H-logdet}.

For the boundary formula, set $w=x+i\varepsilon$.  Then
\[
   \operatorname{Re}H(x+i\varepsilon)
   =
   \int_{\mathbb R}
   \log\sqrt{(t-x)^2+\varepsilon^2}\,
   d\mu_{S_a}(t).
\]
As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, the right-hand side decreases to
\[
   \int_{\mathbb R}\log|t-x|\,d\mu_{S_a}(t)
   =
   \log\Delta(S_a-x),
\]
possibly with value $-\infty$.

If $G(x+i0)$ exists and is invertible, then
\[
   -\frac1m\log|\det G(x+i\varepsilon)|
   +
   \frac12
   \operatorname{Re}
   \operatorname{tr}_m\bigl(
      G(x+i\varepsilon)\eta(G(x+i\varepsilon))
   \bigr)
\]
converges to the right-hand side of
\eqref{eq:closed-boundary}.  This proves the boundary identity.

label: prop:action-identity
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Exact identity on normalized triples

label: eq:normalization
title: Proof
body_md:
Unitarity implies
$M^*bM=MbM^*=b^{-1}$ and $|\det M|=(\det b)^{-1}$. Adding the two
matrix identities gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normalization}
 b^{-1}=ubu+\gamma b\gamma,
 \qquad
 \left\langle u,\mathcal C_{b}u\right\rangle+\left\langle \gamma,\mathcal C_{b}\gamma\right\rangle=1.
\end{equation}
Direct expansion of \eqref{eq:dyson-action} gives
\begin{equation*}
 \operatorname{Re}\mathcal A_{z}(M)
 =\operatorname{tr}_m\log b+\left\langle a_z,u\right\rangle
     -\frac12\left\langle u,\eta(u)\right\rangle
     +\frac12\left\langle \gamma,\eta(\gamma)\right\rangle-1.
\end{equation*}
In \eqref{eq:intro-KK}, the two $\mathcal C_{b}$ terms sum to $-\frac12$ by
\eqref{eq:normalization}. This gives the same expression up to the additive constant $\frac12$ in the statement.
head: environment

label: rem:extended-action
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:extended-action}

 We record three observations.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{No minimax.}

Taking $b=tI$ with $t\downarrow0$
shows that $\inf_{b\succ0}\mathcal{K}_z(b,u,\gamma)=-\infty$ for every
$(u,\gamma)$.  Hence
\[
   \sup_{\substack{u=u^*\\ \gamma\succeq0}}\ \inf_{b\succ0}
   \mathcal{K}_z(b,u,\gamma)
   =-\infty ,
\]
and the order of the extrema in \eqref{eq:intro-F0} and
\eqref{eq:intro-main-formula} cannot be interchanged.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Common critical point and critical value.}
Consider the regularized functional
$\mathcal{K}_{z,\varepsilon}=\mathcal{K}_z+\varepsilon\operatorname{tr}_m\gamma$ of Section~\ref{sec:regularized}.
The computation in the proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:action-identity} gives
$\mathcal{K}_{z,\varepsilon}(b,u,\gamma)=\operatorname{Re}\mathcal A_{z+i\varepsilon}(M)+\frac12$ on normalized
triples.  The stationarity conditions of $\mathcal{K}_{z,\varepsilon}$ in $u$, $\gamma$
and $b$ are
\[
   L_b^+u=a_z,
   \qquad
   L_b^-\gamma=\varepsilon I,
   \qquad
   b^{-1}=ubu+\gamma b\gamma ,
\]
which are the balanced Dyson equations \eqref{eq:balanced}.  

Eliminating a group of variables through its own stationarity condition,
when that condition determines them uniquely and smoothly, changes neither
the critical points nor the critical values of a function.  For
$b\in\mathcal F^{\circ}$, eliminating $(u,\gamma)$ produces the reduced objective
\[
   F_{z,\varepsilon}(b)=\max_{u,\gamma}\mathcal{K}_{z,\varepsilon}(b,u,\gamma).
\]
For $\gamma\succ0$, the function $b\mapsto\mathcal{K}_{z,\varepsilon}(b,u,\gamma)$ is
strictly geodesically concave: $\operatorname{tr}_m\log b$ is affine along geodesics,
and by Lemma~\ref{lem:C-geodesic} the second derivative of
$\langle\gamma,\mathcal C_{b_t}\gamma\rangle$ at $t=0$ is
$\|Xw+wX\|_2^2$ with $w=b^{1/2}\gamma b^{1/2}\succ0$, which is positive
for $X\neq0$.  Its unique critical point is the unitary normalizer of
$-u-i\gamma$, so by Proposition~\ref{prop:action-identity}
\[
   \max_{b\succ0}\mathcal{K}_{z,\varepsilon}(b,u,\gamma)
   =\operatorname{Re}\mathcal A_{z+i\varepsilon}(-u-i\gamma)+\frac12 .
\]
Thus $F_{z,\varepsilon}$ and $\operatorname{Re}\mathcal A_{z+i\varepsilon}+\frac12$ are two reductions of
the same function, and the equality of their critical values is automatic.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Type of the critical point.}
What is not automatic is the nature of the critical point.  Since
$\mathcal A_w$ is holomorphic in $M$, a nondegenerate critical point of
$\operatorname{Re}\mathcal A_w$ has as many negative as positive directions, so the Dyson
action itself admits no extremal characterization of the Dyson solution.
In the extended functional the negative directions are carried by the
auxiliary variables $(u,\gamma)$ and are removed by the inner
maximization.  The remaining problem in $b$ is geodesically convex
(Corollary~\ref{cor:Freg-convex}), and its critical point is a global
minimizer.  This is the reason for introducing the scale $b$ as an
independent variable.

label: lem:feasible-pf
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Perron--Frobenius description of the feasible set

label: eq:normalized-minus
title: Proof
body_md:
Let
$
   T_b:=\mathcal C_{b^{-1/2}}.
$
As an operator on Hilbert--Schmidt space, $T_b$ is self-adjoint, positive
definite, and invertible.  A direct calculation gives
$
   T_b\mathcal C_bT_b=I,
$
and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normalized-minus}
   T_b(\mathcal C_b-\eta)T_b
   =
   I-\widehat\eta_b.
\end{equation}
Since a congruence $A\mapsto T_bAT_b$ by an invertible positive operator
preserves positivity of self-adjoint operators,
\[
   \mathcal C_b-\eta\succeq0
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   I-\widehat\eta_b\succeq0.
\]
Because $\widehat\eta_b$ is Hilbert--Schmidt self-adjoint, the latter is
equivalent to
$
   \lambda_{\max}(\widehat\eta_b)\leq1.
$

We next compare the largest eigenvalue with the operator norm.
The map $\widehat\eta_b$ is positive as a map on matrices, so the
Perron--Frobenius theorem for positive maps \cite{EvansHoeghKrohn1978} implies that its spectral
radius
$
   r(\widehat\eta_b)
$
is an eigenvalue with a positive semidefinite eigenvector.  Since
$\widehat\eta_b$ is Hilbert--Schmidt self-adjoint, its spectrum is real
and
\[
   \|\widehat\eta_b\|
   =
   r(\widehat\eta_b)
   =
   \lambda_{\max}(\widehat\eta_b).
\]
This proves the equivalence of (ii) and (iii).

For a self-adjoint operator, $\|\widehat\eta_b\|\leq1$ is equivalent to
$
   -I\preceq\widehat\eta_b\preceq I,
$
or
$
   I\pm\widehat\eta_b\succeq0.
$
Applying the inverse congruence to
\[
   T_b(\mathcal C_b\pm\eta)T_b
   =
   I\pm\widehat\eta_b
\]
gives (iv).

It remains to identify the interior.  If
$\|\widehat\eta_b\|<1$, continuity in $b$ shows that the same strict
inequality holds in a neighborhood of $b$, so $b\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal{F}$.
Conversely, if $\|\widehat\eta_b\|=1$, then for $0<\lambda<1$,
$
   \widehat\eta_{\lambda b}
   =
   \lambda^{-2}\widehat\eta_b,
$
and hence
\[
   \|\widehat\eta_{\lambda b}\|
   =
   \lambda^{-2}>1.
\]
Thus points outside $\mathcal{F}$ occur arbitrarily close to $b$, so $b$ is a
boundary point.  This proves \eqref{eq:interior-feasible}.
head: environment

label: prop:indicator
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Eliminating the multiplier enforces feasibility

title: Proof
body_md:
If $b\in\mathcal{F}$, then $L_b^-=\mathcal C_b-\eta\succeq0$ on the whole
Hilbert--Schmidt space, so every quantity in the supremum is
nonpositive, and $\gamma=0$ gives the value $0$.

Let $b\notin\mathcal{F}$.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:feasible-pf},
$\|\widehat\eta_b\|>1$.  The map $\widehat\eta_b$ is positive, so by the
Perron--Frobenius theorem for positive maps \cite{EvansHoeghKrohn1978}
its spectral radius $r$ is an eigenvalue with a positive semidefinite
eigenvector: there is $Q\succeq0$, $Q\neq0$, with
$\widehat\eta_b(Q)=rQ$.  Since $\widehat\eta_b$ is Hilbert--Schmidt
self-adjoint, $r=\|\widehat\eta_b\|>1$.

Put $\gamma_0:=b^{-1/2}Qb^{-1/2}\succeq0$.  Then
$\mathcal C_b(\gamma_0)=b^{1/2}Qb^{1/2}$, and by the definition
\eqref{eq:eta-hat} of $\widehat\eta_b$,
\[
 \left\langle \gamma_0,\mathcal C_b\gamma_0\right\rangle=\left\langle Q,Q\right\rangle,
 \qquad
 \left\langle \gamma_0,\eta(\gamma_0)\right\rangle
 =\left\langle Q,\widehat\eta_b(Q)\right\rangle
 =r\left\langle Q,Q\right\rangle.
\]
Hence $\left\langle \gamma_0,L_b^-\gamma_0\right\rangle=(1-r)\left\langle Q,Q\right\rangle<0$.  For $t>0$ we
have $t\gamma_0\succeq0$ and
\[
 -\frac12\left\langle t\gamma_0,L_b^-(t\gamma_0)\right\rangle
 =\frac{t^2}{2}(r-1)\left\langle Q,Q\right\rangle\longrightarrow+\infty
 \qquad(t\to\infty).
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:indicator}.

For fixed $b\succ0$, $\mathscr K_z(b,u,\gamma)$ is the sum of $\operatorname{tr}_m\log b$,
a function of $u$ alone, and a function of $\gamma$ alone.  Therefore
\[
 \sup_{\substack{u=u^*\\\gamma\succeq0}}\mathscr K_z(b,u,\gamma)
 =\operatorname{tr}_m\log b
  +\sup_{u=u^*}\Bigl\{\left\langle a_z,u\right\rangle-\frac12\left\langle u,L_b^+u\right\rangle\Bigr\}
  +\sup_{\gamma\succeq0}\Bigl\{-\frac12\left\langle \gamma,L_b^-\gamma\right\rangle\Bigr\}.
\]
The supremum over $u$ is at least $0$ (take $u=0$), so the right-hand
side is well defined in $(-\infty,+\infty]$.  By \eqref{eq:indicator}
and \eqref{eq:intro-F}, it equals $F_z(b)$ for $b\in\mathcal{F}$ and $+\infty$
for $b\notin\mathcal{F}$.  Taking the infimum over $b\succ0$ gives
\eqref{eq:three-variable-real}; the order of the extrema is unchanged.

label: lem:radial-approximation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:radial-approximation}
Let $b\in\mathcal{F}$.  Then
$
   \lambda b\in\mathcal F^\circ$ for every $\lambda>1$,
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:radial-limit}
   F_z(\lambda b)
   \longrightarrow
   F_z(b)
   \qquad
   (\lambda\downarrow1)
\end{equation}
in the extended-real sense.
head: environment
name: Radial approximation of boundary values

title: Proof
body_md:
Since
$
   \mathcal C_{\lambda b}
   =
   \lambda^2\mathcal C_b,
$
we have
\[
   \mathcal C_{\lambda b}-\eta
   =
   (\lambda^2-1)\mathcal C_b
   +
   (\mathcal C_b-\eta)
   \succ0.
\]
Thus $\lambda b\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal{F}$.

Write
$
   F_z(b)=\operatorname{tr}_m\log b+Q_z(b),
$
where
\[
   Q_z(b)
   :=
   \sup_{u=u^*}
   \left\{
      \left\langle a_z,u\right\rangle-\frac12\left\langle u,L_b^+ u\right\rangle
   \right\}
   \in[0,+\infty].
\]
  Since
\[
   L_{\lambda b}^+
   =
   L_b^+ +(\lambda^2-1)\mathcal C_b,
\]
we have
\begin{align*}
   Q_z(\lambda b)
   =
   \sup_{u=u^*}
   \biggl\{
      \left\langle a_z,u\right\rangle
      -
      \frac12\left\langle u,L_b^+ u\right\rangle
      -
      \frac{\lambda^2-1}{2}
      \left\langle u,\mathcal C_bu\right\rangle
   \biggr\}.
\end{align*}

For each fixed $u$, the expression in braces increases to
$\left\langle a_z,u\right\rangle-\frac12\left\langle u,L_b^+u\right\rangle$ as $\lambda\downarrow1$, because
$\left\langle u,\mathcal C_bu\right\rangle\ge0$.  Hence $Q_z(\lambda b)$ is nondecreasing as
$\lambda\downarrow1$, its limit is the supremum over $\lambda>1$, and the
two suprema may be interchanged:
\[
   \lim_{\lambda\downarrow1}Q_z(\lambda b)
   =\sup_{\lambda>1}\,\sup_{u=u^*}\{\cdots\}
   =\sup_{u=u^*}\,\sup_{\lambda>1}\{\cdots\}
   =Q_z(b)
\]
in the extended-real sense, including the case $Q_z(b)=+\infty$.
Finally,
\[
   \operatorname{tr}_m\log(\lambda b)
   =
   \log\lambda+\operatorname{tr}_m\log b
   \longrightarrow
   \operatorname{tr}_m\log b,
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:radial-limit}.
head: environment

label: lem:C-geodesic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:C-geodesic}
Let
$
   b_t=b^{1/2}e^{tX}b^{1/2},$
   with
   $X=X^*,$
and define the self-adjoint operator on Hilbert--Schmidt space $B$:
\[
   D_X(Y):=XY+YX.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C-geodesic}
   \mathcal C_{b_t}
   =
   \mathcal C_{b^{1/2}}\,
   e^{tD_X}\,
   \mathcal C_{b^{1/2}}.
\end{equation}
Hence $t\mapsto\mathcal C_{b_t}$ is a geodesic in the cone of positive
definite operators on Hilbert--Schmidt space $B$.  In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C-geodesic-equation}
   \mathcal C_{b_t}''
   =
   \mathcal C_{b_t}'
   \mathcal C_{b_t}^{-1}
   \mathcal C_{b_t}'.
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: $\mathcal C$ maps geodesics to geodesics

title: Proof
body_md:
Left and right multiplication by $X$ commute, and therefore
\[
   e^{tD_X}(Y)
   =
   e^{tX}Ye^{tX}
   =
   \mathcal C_{e^{tX}}(Y).
\]
Since
$
   \mathcal C_{b_t}
   =
   \mathcal C_{b^{1/2}}
   \mathcal C_{e^{tX}}
   \mathcal C_{b^{1/2}},
$
this proves \eqref{eq:C-geodesic}.

Write
$
   P:=\mathcal C_{b^{1/2}},$ and 
   $
   D:=D_X.
$
Then
$
   \mathcal C_{b_t}=Pe^{tD}P,
$
so
\[
   \mathcal C_{b_t}'
   =
   PDe^{tD}P,
   \qquad
   \mathcal C_{b_t}''
   =
   PD^2e^{tD}P.
\]
Since
$
   \mathcal C_{b_t}^{-1}
   =
   P^{-1}e^{-tD}P^{-1},
$
we obtain
\begin{align*}
   \mathcal C_{b_t}'
   \mathcal C_{b_t}^{-1}
   \mathcal C_{b_t}'
   &=
   PDe^{tD}P
   P^{-1}e^{-tD}P^{-1}
   PDe^{tD}P  \\
   &=
   PD^2e^{tD}P
   =
   \mathcal C_{b_t}''.
\end{align*}
head: environment

label: lem:geodesic-feasible
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Geodesic log-convexity of the normalized covariance

label: eq:eta-quotient
title: Proof
body_md:
Let
\[
   W:=e^{D_X}\succ0,
   \qquad
   \Phi:=\widehat\eta_{b_0}.
\]
By \eqref{eq:C-geodesic},
$
   \mathcal C_{b_t}
   =
   \mathcal C_{b_0^{1/2}}
   W^t
   \mathcal C_{b_0^{1/2}}.
$

For $b\succ0$, introduce the weighted norm
\[
   \|Y\|_{\mathcal C_b}^2
   :=
   \left\langle Y,\mathcal C_bY\right\rangle.
\]
A change of variables in the Hilbert--Schmidt operator norm gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:eta-quotient}
   \|\widehat\eta_b\|
   =
   \sup_{Y,Z\neq0}
   \frac{
      |\left\langle Y,\eta(Z)\right\rangle|
   }{
      \|Y\|_{\mathcal C_b}
      \|Z\|_{\mathcal C_b}
   }.
\end{equation}
Applying this to $b_t$ and changing variables by
$\mathcal C_{b_0^{-1/2}}$ gives
\[
   \|\widehat\eta_{b_t}\|
   =
   \bigl\|
      W^{-t/2}\Phi W^{-t/2}
   \bigr\|.
\]

Now consider
\[
   f(\zeta)
   :=
   W^{-\zeta/2}\Phi W^{-\zeta/2},
   \qquad
   0\leq\operatorname{Re}\zeta\leq1.
\]
Since $W\succ0$, the complex powers are well defined and $f$ is analytic
in the strip.  On the line $\operatorname{Re}\zeta=0$,
$W^{-is/2}$ is unitary, so
\[
   \|f(is)\|=\|\Phi\|=\|\widehat\eta_{b_0}\|.
\]
Similarly,
\[
   \|f(1+is)\|
   =
   \|W^{-1/2}\Phi W^{-1/2}\|
   =
   \|\widehat\eta_{b_1}\|.
\]

Fix unit vectors $u, v$ in Hilbert--Schmidt space and apply
Hadamard's three-lines theorem to the scalar analytic function
\[
   \zeta\longmapsto
   \left\langle u,f(\zeta)v\right\rangle.
\]
Taking the supremum over the two unit vectors gives
\eqref{eq:eta-geodesic-logconvex}.

If $b_0,b_1\in\mathcal{F}$, then both endpoint norms are at most $1$, hence
$
   \|\widehat\eta_{b_t}\|\leq1,
$
and $b_t\in\mathcal{F}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:feasible-pf}.  If in addition
$b_1\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal{F}$, then
$\|\widehat\eta_{b_1}\|<1$, and for every $t>0$,
$
   \|\widehat\eta_{b_t}\|
   \leq
   \|\widehat\eta_{b_1}\|^t
   <1.
$
Thus $b_t\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal{F}$.

label: cor:two-inverse-geodesic
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Geodesic convexity of both inverse terms

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:C-geodesic}, $t\mapsto\mathcal C_t$ is an
operator geodesic. By Lemma~\ref{lem:feasible-pf},
$\|\widehat\eta_t\|<1$, so $I\pm\widehat\eta_t\succ0$ and
$L_{b_t}^\pm\succ0$.

Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:resolvent-geodesic} with
$\Theta=\eta$ and $\Theta=-\eta$, respectively. This gives
\eqref{eq:two-inverse-hessian}. Both middle factors are positive
definite: for $-1<\lambda<1$, the numbers
$(1-\lambda)/(1+\lambda)$ and $(1+\lambda)/(1-\lambda)$ are positive.
Pairing \eqref{eq:two-inverse-hessian} with the fixed vector $v$
proves the assertion about $q_v^\pm$.

The use of $\Theta=-\eta$ requires only self-adjointness of the
shift in the abstract lemma; it does not assert that $-\eta$ is a
positive map.
head: environment

label: prop:geodesic-hessian
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Geodesic Hessian of $F_z$

title: Proof
body_md:
On $\operatorname{int}\mathcal F$,
\begin{equation*}
   F_z(b)=\operatorname{tr}_m\log b+q_{a_z}^+(b).
\end{equation*}
The quadratic term is geodesically convex by
Corollary~\ref{cor:two-inverse-geodesic}. The logarithmic term is
affine along geodesics:
\begin{equation*}
   \operatorname{tr}_m\log b_t
   =\operatorname{tr}_m\log b
      +t\,\operatorname{tr}_mX.
\end{equation*}
This proves geodesic convexity of $F_z$.

For the explicit Hessian, put
$h:=\dot b_0=b^{1/2}Xb^{1/2}$ and
$\mathcal C_t:=\mathcal C_{b_t}$. Then
\begin{equation*}
   \mathcal C_0'(Y)=hYb+bYh.
\end{equation*}
The logarithmic term has zero second derivative, so the plus case
of \eqref{eq:two-inverse-hessian} gives
\begin{equation*}
   \left.\frac{d^2}{dt^2}F_z(b_t)\right|_{t=0}
   =\frac12\left\langle
      K_+(0)a_z,\,
      (I-\widehat\eta_b)(I+\widehat\eta_b)^{-1}K_+(0)a_z
   \right\rangle.
\end{equation*}
Since $\mathcal C_b^{-1/2}=\mathcal C_{b^{-1/2}}$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
   K_+(0)a_z
   &=\mathcal C_b^{-1/2}\mathcal C_0'u\\
   &=b^{-1/2}(hub+buh)b^{-1/2}\\
   &=Xb^{1/2}ub^{1/2}+b^{1/2}ub^{1/2}X\\
   &=X\widetilde u+\widetilde uX.
\end{align*}
Substitution proves \eqref{eq:geodesic-hessian}. 

Since this second derivative is nonnegative, $F_z$ is geodesically convex on $\mathcal F^{\circ}$. For the points on the boundary, we can approximate: $(\lambda b_0) \#_t (\lambda b_1) = \lambda (b_0 \#_t b_1)$ is interior for $\lambda > 1$; let $\lambda \downarrow 1$ with Lemma \ref{lem:radial-approximation}.

label: def:unitary-normalizer
title: Definition
head: environment
name: Unitary normalizer

label: lem:pup
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:pup}
Let
\[
   G=X-iY,
   \qquad
   X=X^*,
   \qquad
   Y\succ0.
\]
Set
\[
   T:=Y^{-1/2}XY^{-1/2}
\]
and define $b_*\succ0$ by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pup-b}
   b_*^{-1}
   :=
   Y^{1/2}
   \bigl(I+T^2\bigr)^{1/2}
   Y^{1/2}.
\end{equation}
Then $b_*$ is a unitary normalizer of $G$.

Equivalently, every matrix with strictly negative imaginary part admits a
factorization
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pup}
   G=pUp,
   \qquad
   p\succ0,
   \qquad
   U\in U(m),
\end{equation}
with $p=b_*^{-1/2}$. The factorization is unique: if $b$ is a unitary normalizer of $G$, then $b=b_*$.

For $m=1$,
$
   b_*=|G|^{-1}.
$
head: environment
name: $pUp$ factorization

title: Proof
body_md:
Since
$
   G
   =
   Y^{1/2}(T-iI)Y^{1/2},
$
it is enough first to factor $T-iI$.

Because $T=T^*$, the matrices $T$ and $I+T^2$ commute.  Define
\[
   A:=(I+T^2)^{1/4}
\]
and
\[
   U_0
   :=
   (T-iI)(I+T^2)^{-1/2}.
\]
Then
\[
   T-iI
   =
   A\,U_0\,A.
\]
Moreover,
\begin{align*}
   U_0^*U_0
   &=
   (I+T^2)^{-1/2}
   (T+iI)(T-iI)
   (I+T^2)^{-1/2} \\
   &=
   I,
\end{align*}
so $U_0$ is unitary.

Hence
$
   G
   =
   L\,U_0\,L^*,$ where
  $ L:=Y^{1/2}A. $
Take the polar decomposition
\[
   L=pV,
   \qquad
   p:=(LL^*)^{1/2}\succ0,
   \qquad
   V\in U(m).
\]
Then
\[
   G
   =
   p\,(VU_0V^*)\,p,
\]
and $VU_0V^*$ is unitary.  Thus \eqref{eq:pup} holds.

Finally,
\[
   p^2
   =
   LL^*
   =
   Y^{1/2}
   (I+T^2)^{1/2}
   Y^{1/2}.
\]
Since $p=b_*^{-1/2}$, this is precisely
\eqref{eq:pup-b}.

For uniqueness, let $b$ be any unitary normalizer of $G$.  By
\eqref{eq:normalizer-inverse}, $G^{-1}=bG^*b=b(X+iY)b$, so
\[
   bYb=\operatorname{Im}\bigl(G^{-1}\bigr)
   :=\frac{1}{2i}\bigl(G^{-1}-(G^{-1})^*\bigr).
\]
Since $Y\succ0$, the right-hand side is positive definite, and the
equation $bYb=N$ with $Y,N\succ0$ has the unique positive definite
solution $b=Y^{-1/2}\bigl(Y^{1/2}NY^{1/2}\bigr)^{1/2}Y^{-1/2}$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The formula \eqref{eq:pup-b} is the noncommutative analogue of the scalar
identity
\[
   |x-iy|
   =
   y
   \sqrt{
      1+\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)^2
   }.
\]
Thus $b_*^{-1}$ plays the role of the modulus of $G$, but in a form adapted
to symmetric congruence rather than to the ordinary polar decomposition.

label: lem:balanced-dyson-parts
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:balanced-dyson-parts}
Let
$
   w=x+i\varepsilon,$
   with
   $\varepsilon\geq0,
$
and suppose that
\[
   G:=G(w)
   =
   -u-i\gamma,
   \qquad
   u=u^*,
   \qquad
   \gamma=\gamma^*\succeq0,
\]
is invertible.  Let $b\succ0$ be a unitary normalizer of $G$.  Then
\begin{align}
   (\mathcal C_b+\eta)(u)
   &=
   a_x,
   \label{eq:dyson-real-unbalanced}\\
   (\mathcal C_b-\eta)(\gamma)
   &=
   \varepsilon I,
   \label{eq:dyson-imag-unbalanced}
\end{align}
where
$
   a_x:=a-xI.
$
head: environment
name: Real and imaginary parts of the balanced Dyson equation

label: eq:normalizer-parts
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $b$ is a unitary normalizer,
$
   G^{-1}=bG^*b.
$
Using
\[
   G=-u-i\gamma,
   \qquad
   G^*=-u+i\gamma,
\]
we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normalizer-parts}
   G^{-1}
   =
   -bub+i\,b\gamma b.
\end{equation}

On the other hand, the Dyson equation gives
\[
   G^{-1}
   =
   wI-a-\eta(G).
\]
Since
$
   wI-a
   =
   -a_x+i\varepsilon I
$
and
$
   \eta(G)
   =
   -\eta(u)-i\eta(\gamma),
$
we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dyson-parts}
   G^{-1}
   =
   -a_x+\eta(u)
   +
   i\bigl(
      \varepsilon I+\eta(\gamma)
   \bigr).
\end{equation}

Comparing the real parts of
\eqref{eq:normalizer-parts} and
\eqref{eq:dyson-parts} gives
\[
   bub+\eta(u)=a_x,
\]
which is \eqref{eq:dyson-real-unbalanced}.  Comparing imaginary parts gives
$
   b\gamma b
   =
   \varepsilon I+\eta(\gamma),
$
or equivalently
\[
   (\mathcal C_b-\eta)(\gamma)
   =
   \varepsilon I.
\]
This is \eqref{eq:dyson-imag-unbalanced}.

label: cor:balanced-dyson
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Balanced Dyson equations

label: eq:PQ-ugamma
title: Proof
body_md:
Since
$
   G=-u-i\gamma
$
and
$
   U=b^{1/2}Gb^{1/2}=P-iQ,
$
we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:PQ-ugamma}
   P
   =
   -b^{1/2}ub^{1/2},
   \qquad
   Q
   =
   b^{1/2}\gamma b^{1/2}.
\end{equation}

Apply the congruence map
$\mathcal C_{b^{-1/2}}$ to
\eqref{eq:dyson-real-unbalanced}.  Since
$
   u
   =
   -b^{-1/2}Pb^{-1/2},
$
we obtain
\[
   -P-\widehat\eta_b(P)
   =
   \widetilde a_{x,b}.
\]
This is \eqref{eq:balanced-real}.

Similarly, applying
$\mathcal C_{b^{-1/2}}$ to
\eqref{eq:dyson-imag-unbalanced} and using
$
   \gamma
   =
   b^{-1/2}Qb^{-1/2}
$
gives
\[
   Q-\widehat\eta_b(Q)
   =
   \varepsilon b^{-1},
\]
which is \eqref{eq:balanced-imag}.
head: environment

label: rem:two-stability-operators
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:two-stability-operators}
The balanced Dyson equations explain the appearance of the two operators
\[
   I+\widehat\eta_b
   \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   I-\widehat\eta_b
\]
in the variational problem.

The real part of the Dyson solution is determined through
$I+\widehat\eta_b$, while its imaginary part is controlled by
$I-\widehat\eta_b$.  In particular, at a real boundary point
$\varepsilon=0$,
\[
   (I-\widehat\eta_b)Q=0.
\]
Thus a nonzero imaginary part of the boundary Dyson solution produces a
nontrivial kernel of the stability operator
$I-\widehat\eta_b$, and hence an active feasibility constraint for the limiting scale $b_z$.
head: environment
name: Two stability operators

label: prop:elimination
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: The regularized partial supremum

title: Proof
body_md:
For $b\in\mathcal F^{\circ}$, both $L_b^+$ and $L_b^-$ are positive definite
as Hilbert--Schmidt operators. Completing the square in the two
Hermitian variables gives the unconstrained maximizers
\eqref{eq:maximizers} and the value \eqref{eq:partial-sup}.
It remains to check that the second maximizer is positive definite.

Write
$\widehat\eta_b=\mathcal C_{b^{-1/2}}\eta\mathcal C_{b^{-1/2}}$.
The congruence identities give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:positive-inverse}
 (L_b^-)^{-1}
 =\mathcal C_{b^{-1/2}}
   (\mathrm{id}-\widehat\eta_b)^{-1}
   \mathcal C_{b^{-1/2}},
 \qquad
 (\mathrm{id}-\widehat\eta_b)^{-1}
 =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\widehat\eta_b^{\,k}.
\end{equation}
The series converges because $\|\widehat\eta_b\|_{2\to2}<1$.
Each summand is a positive map. On applying the full expression to
$I$, its zeroth summand is $b^{-2}$. Consequently,
\begin{equation*}
 (L_b^-)^{-1}I\succeq b^{-2}\succ0.
\end{equation*}
Hence $\gamma_b\succ0$: the positivity restriction on $\gamma$
does not change the maximizer or its value.

Now suppose that $b\notin\mathcal F^{\circ}$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:feasible-pf}, the map $\widehat\eta_b$ has a
nonzero positive semidefinite eigenmatrix $P$ with
$\widehat\eta_b(P)=rP$, where
$r=\|\widehat\eta_b\|_{2\to2}\geq1$.
Put $\gamma_0=b^{-1/2}Pb^{-1/2}\succeq0$. Then
\begin{equation*}
 \left\langle \gamma_0,L_b^-\gamma_0\right\rangle
 =(1-r)\|P\|_2^2,
 \qquad \operatorname{tr}_m\gamma_0>0.
\end{equation*}
Taking $u=0$ and $\gamma=t\gamma_0$ gives
\begin{equation*}
 \mathcal{K}_{z,\varepsilon}(b,0,t\gamma_0)
 =\operatorname{tr}_m\log b
   +\frac{t^2}{2}(r-1)\|P\|_2^2
   +\varepsilon t\operatorname{tr}_m\gamma_0.
\end{equation*}
This tends to $+\infty$ as $t\to\infty$, whether $r>1$ or $r=1$.
head: environment

label: lem:Dyson-scale
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Unitary normalization and strict feasibility

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:pup}, applied with $X=-u_\varepsilon$ and $Y=\gamma_\varepsilon$,
the normalizer $b_\varepsilon$ exists, and by \eqref{eq:normalizer-inverse},
$G_\varepsilon^{-1}=b_\varepsilon G_\varepsilon^*b_\varepsilon$.  The Dyson equation and this identity
give two expressions for the inverse: 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
 G_\varepsilon^{-1}
 &=-a_z+\eta(u_\varepsilon)
        +i\bigl(\varepsilonI+\eta(\gamma_\varepsilon)\bigr),\\
 G_\varepsilon^{-1}
 &=-b_\varepsilon u_\varepsilon b_\varepsilon+i b_\varepsilon\gamma_\varepsilon b_\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
Comparing real and imaginary parts yields the first two equations in
\eqref{eq:balanced}. Adding
$G_\varepsilon^*b_\varepsilon G_\varepsilon=b_\varepsilon^{-1}$ and
$G_\varepsilon b_\varepsilon G_\varepsilon^*=b_\varepsilon^{-1}$ cancels the mixed terms
and gives the third equation.

To prove strict feasibility, put
$Q=b_\varepsilon^{1/2}\gamma_\varepsilon b_\varepsilon^{1/2}\succ0$.
Conjugating the imaginary equation gives
\begin{equation*}
 Q-\widehat\eta_{b_\varepsilon}(Q)=\varepsilon b_\varepsilon^{-1}.
\end{equation*}
Choose a nonzero $P_0\succeq0$ with
$\widehat\eta_{b_\varepsilon}(P_0)=rP_0$ and
$r=\|\widehat\eta_{b_\varepsilon}\|_{2\to2}$, as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:feasible-pf}. Hilbert--Schmidt self-adjointness gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
 \varepsilon\left\langle P_0,b_\varepsilon^{-1}\right\rangle
 &=\left\langle P_0,Q\right\rangle-\left\langle P_0,\widehat\eta_{b_\varepsilon}(Q)\right\rangle\\
 &=\left\langle P_0,Q\right\rangle-\left\langle \widehat\eta_{b_\varepsilon}(P_0),Q\right\rangle\\
 &=(1-r)\left\langle P_0,Q\right\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
Both pairings are strictly positive, since $P_0$ is nonzero and
positive semidefinite, whereas $Q$ and $b_\varepsilon^{-1}$ are positive
definite. Therefore $r<1$, so $b_\varepsilon\in\mathcal F^{\circ}$.
Now $L_{b_\varepsilon}^\pm$ are invertible. The first two equations of
\eqref{eq:balanced} uniquely determine $u_\varepsilon$ and $\gamma_\varepsilon$
and coincide with \eqref{eq:maximizers}, proving
\eqref{eq:Dyson-auxiliary-identification}.

head: environment
name: Relation with the formula

label: thm:real-axis
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Real-axis variational identity

label: eq:pointwise-limit
title: Proof
body_md:
For each fixed $b\in\mathcal F^{\circ}$, positivity of $(L_b^-)^{-1}$ as a
Hilbert--Schmidt operator gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pointwise-limit}
 F_{z,\varepsilon}(b)
 =F_z(b)+\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}\left\langle I,(L_b^-)^{-1}I\right\rangle
 \downarrow F_z(b)
 \quad(\varepsilon\downarrow0).
\end{equation}
Put $m_\varepsilon=\inf_{\mathcal F^{\circ}}F_{z,\varepsilon}$ and
$m_0=\inf_{\mathcal F^{\circ}}F_z$. These infima are bounded above by the value
at a fixed strictly feasible matrix, for instance a sufficiently large
multiple of $I$. The numbers $m_\varepsilon$ decrease as
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and satisfy $m_\varepsilon\geq m_0$. Conversely, for
every fixed $b\in\mathcal F^{\circ}$,
\begin{equation*}
 \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}m_\varepsilon
 \leq\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}F_{z,\varepsilon}(b)=F_z(b).
\end{equation*}
Taking the infimum over $b$ proves
\begin{equation}\label{eq:inf-limit}
 \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}m_\varepsilon=m_0,
\end{equation}
including when $m_0=-\infty$. This step uses fixed competitors, not
compactness of minimizing sequences.

On the spectral side,
\begin{equation*}
 \log\Delta(S_a-z-i\varepsilon)
 =\frac12\int_\mathbb{R}\log\bigl((t-z)^2+\varepsilon^2\bigr)\,d\mu(t)
 \downarrow\log\Delta(S_a-z).
\end{equation*}
To justify the limit even when it is $-\infty$, subtract the logarithm
from a fixed upper bound valid for $0<\varepsilon\leq1$ on the compact
support of $\mu$, and apply monotone convergence.

Passing to the limit in Theorem~\ref{thm:regularized}, using
\eqref{eq:inf-limit} and Lemma~\ref{lem:radial-approximation}, proves
\eqref{eq:real-theorem}.
head: environment

label: cor:minus-infinity-atoms
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:minus-infinity-atoms}
For every $z\in\mathbb R$,
\begin{equation*}
   \log\Delta(S_a-z)=-\infty
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   \inf_{b\in\mathcal F}F_z(b)=-\infty
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   \mu_{S_a}(\{z\})>0.
\end{equation*}
In particular, both quantities in the real-axis variational
identity are finite at every non-atomic point.
head: environment
name: Characterization of the value $-\infty$

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:real-axis},
\begin{equation*}
   \inf_{b\in\mathcal F}F_z(b)
   =
   \log\Delta(S_a-z)+\frac12.
\end{equation*}
Thus it suffices to characterize when
\begin{equation*}
   \log\Delta(S_a-z)
   =
   \int_{\mathbb R}\log|t-z|\,d\mu_{S_a}(t)
\end{equation*}
equals $-\infty$. Write $\mu:=\mu_{S_a}$.

Suppose first that $\mu(\{z\})>0$.
The integrand equals $-\infty$ on a set of positive
$\mu$-measure. Its positive part is integrable because
$\mu$ has compact support. Hence
$\log\Delta(S_a-z)=-\infty$.

Conversely, suppose that $\mu(\{z\})=0$.
By Theorem~\ref{thm:nonatomic-local-regularity}, there exist
$0<r<1$, an exponent $1<p<\infty$, and a nonnegative
function $\rho\in L^p(J)$, where $J=(z-r,z+r)$, such that
\begin{equation*}
   d\mu(t)\big|_J=\rho(t)\,dt.
\end{equation*}
Let $q=p/(p-1)$. H\"older's inequality gives
\begin{align*}
   \int_J|\log|t-z||\,d\mu(t)
   &=
   \int_J|\log|t-z||\,\rho(t)\,dt\\
   &\leq
   \|\rho\|_{L^p(J)}
   \left(
      \int_{-r}^{r}|\log|s||^q\,ds
   \right)^{1/q}
   <\infty.
\end{align*}
The last integral is finite since
\begin{equation*}
   \int_{-r}^{r}|\log|s||^q\,ds
   =
   2\int_{\log(1/r)}^\infty y^q e^{-y}\,dy
   <\infty.
\end{equation*}
On $\operatorname{supp}\mu\setminus J$, the function
$t\mapsto|\log|t-z||$ is bounded, because the support is
compact and $|t-z|\geq r$. Therefore
\begin{equation*}
   \int_{\mathbb R}|\log|t-z||\,d\mu(t)<\infty,
\end{equation*}
so $\log\Delta(S_a-z)$ is finite. The variational identity
then gives finiteness of $\inf_{b\in\mathcal F}F_z(b)$
as well.

label: prop:attainment-cluster-point
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:attainment-cluster-point}
Fix $z\in\mathbb R$, and let $b_\varepsilon$ be the
regularized Dyson scales. Suppose that, for some sequence
$\varepsilon_k\downarrow0$,
$
   b_{\varepsilon_k}\longrightarrow b_*\succ0.
$
Then $b_*\in\mathcal F$, the infimum
$
   m_z:=\inf_{b\in\mathcal F}F_z(b)
$
is finite, and
$
   F_z(b_*)=m_z.
$

In particular, if $m_z=-\infty$, the regularized scales
have no positive definite cluster point as
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$.
head: environment
name: Attainment at a positive definite cluster point

label: eq:attainment-minimizing-family
title: Proof
body_md:
We first recall why the regularized scales form a minimizing
family for the unregularized objective. Put
\begin{equation*}
   m_\varepsilon
   :=
   \min_{b\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal F}
      F_{z,\varepsilon}(b).
\end{equation*}
The real-axis limiting argument gives
$m_\varepsilon\to m_z$. Since the regularization term is
nonnegative and $b_\varepsilon$ minimizes
$F_{z,\varepsilon}$,
\begin{equation*}
   m_z
   \leq F_z(b_\varepsilon)
   \leq F_{z,\varepsilon}(b_\varepsilon)
   =m_\varepsilon.
\end{equation*}
It follows that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:attainment-minimizing-family}
   F_z(b_\varepsilon)\longrightarrow m_z
   \qquad(\varepsilon\downarrow0),
\end{equation}
also when $m_z=-\infty$.

Next, $b_{\varepsilon_k}\in\mathcal F$ and continuity of
$b\mapsto\mathcal C_b$ give
\begin{equation*}
   \mathcal C_{b_*}-\eta
   =
   \lim_{k\to\infty}
   \bigl(\mathcal C_{b_{\varepsilon_k}}-\eta\bigr)
   \succeq0.
\end{equation*}
Because $b_*\succ0$, this proves $b_*\in\mathcal F$.

We use the supremum definition to pass to the limit in the
objective, without assuming that $L_{b_*}^+$ is invertible.
For every fixed Hermitian matrix $u$, set
\begin{equation*}
   \ell_z(b,u)
   :=
   \operatorname{tr}_m\log b
   +\langle a_z,u\rangle
   -\frac12\langle u,L_b^+u\rangle.
\end{equation*}
The function $b\mapsto\ell_z(b,u)$ is continuous on the
positive definite cone, and
\begin{equation*}
   F_z(b)=\sup_{u=u^*}\ell_z(b,u),
   \qquad b\in\mathcal F.
\end{equation*}
Therefore, for every fixed $u=u^*$,
\begin{equation*}
   \ell_z(b_*,u)
   =
   \lim_{k\to\infty}\ell_z(b_{\varepsilon_k},u)
   \leq
   \liminf_{k\to\infty}F_z(b_{\varepsilon_k}).
\end{equation*}
Taking the supremum over $u$ proves lower semicontinuity
along this sequence:
\begin{equation*}
   F_z(b_*)
   \leq
   \liminf_{k\to\infty}F_z(b_{\varepsilon_k})
   =m_z.
\end{equation*}

Taking $u=0$ in the supremum definition gives
\begin{equation*}
   F_z(b_*)\geq\operatorname{tr}_m\log b_*>-\infty.
\end{equation*}
Hence $m_z=-\infty$ is impossible under the cluster-point
hypothesis. Moreover, $m_z<+\infty$, since $F_z$ is finite
at any strictly feasible matrix. Thus $m_z$ is finite.
Finally, feasibility of $b_*$ gives the reverse inequality
$m_z\leq F_z(b_*)$, and therefore
$
   F_z(b_*)=m_z.
$
head: environment

label: prop:normalizer-limit
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:normalizer-limit}
Suppose that
$
   G:=G(z+i0)
$
exists.

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)]
If
$
   -\operatorname{Im}G\succ0,
$
then
$
   b_\varepsilon\longrightarrow b_z,
$
where $b_z$ is the unitary normalizer obtained by applying the $pUp$
formula of Lemma~\ref{lem:pup} directly to $G$.

\item[(ii)]
Suppose that $z$ belongs to an open component of
$\mathbb R\setminus\operatorname{supp}\mu_{S_a}$.  Then $G(z)=G(z)^*$, and
$
   b_\varepsilon\longrightarrow b_z,
$
where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gap-normalizer}
   b_z^{-1}
   =
   D^{1/2}
   \left|
      D^{-1/2}G(z)D^{-1/2}
   \right|
   D^{1/2},
   \qquad
   D:=-G'(z)\succ0.
\end{equation}
The matrix $b_z$ is a unitary normalizer of $G(z)$.  If $G(z)$ is
definite, in particular on either unbounded component of the resolvent
set, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:definite-normalizer}
   b_z=|G(z)|^{-1}.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Limit of the regularized normalizers

label: cor:regularized-value-limit
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:regularized-value-limit}
Fix $z\in\mathbb R$. Suppose that the finite boundary value
\begin{equation*}
   G:=G(z+i0)
   =
   \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}G(z+i\varepsilon)
\end{equation*}
exists, and that either $-\operatorname{Im}G\succ0$ or $z$
belongs to an open component of
$\mathbb R\setminus\operatorname{supp}\mu_{S_a}$.

Let $b_z$ be the limiting scale from
Proposition~\ref{prop:normalizer-limit}.
Then $b_z\in\mathcal F$, the infimum of $F_z$ on
$\mathcal F$ is finite and attained at $b_z$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:value-limiting-scale}
   F_z(b_z)
   =
   \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}F_z(b_\varepsilon)
   =
   \log\Delta(S_a-z)+\frac12.
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: Attainment at nondegenerate regular points

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{prop:normalizer-limit},
$b_\varepsilon\to b_z\succ0$. Hence
Proposition~\ref{prop:attainment-cluster-point} gives
$b_z\in\mathcal F$ and
\begin{equation*}
   F_z(b_z)=\inf_{b\in\mathcal F}F_z(b)\in\mathbb R.
\end{equation*}
The regularized scales form a minimizing family for $F_z$,
so $F_z(b_\varepsilon)$ converges to this infimum.
Finally, Theorem~\ref{thm:real-axis} identifies the infimum
with $\log\Delta(S_a-z)+\frac12$, proving
\eqref{eq:value-limiting-scale}.
head: environment

label: prop:active-set
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:active-set}
Fix $z\in\mathbb R$ and let $b_\varepsilon$ be the regularized scales.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)]
Suppose that $G:=G(z+i0)$ exists, that
$\operatorname{Im}G\neq0$, and that
$b_{\varepsilon_k}\to b_*\succ0$ for some sequence
$\varepsilon_k\downarrow0$.  Then $b_*\in\partial\mathcal F$.  In
particular, if $-\operatorname{Im}G\succ0$, then
$b_z\in\partial\mathcal F$.

\item[(ii)]
Suppose that $z$ belongs to an open component of
$\mathbb R\setminus\operatorname{supp}\mu_{S_a}$.  Then
$b_z\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal F$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gap-stability}
   \bigl(\mathcal C_{b_z}-\eta\bigr)(D)=I,
   \qquad
   D=-G'(z)\succ0.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, at a nondegenerate regular point $z$,
\begin{equation*}
   b_z\in\partial\mathcal F
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   z\in\operatorname{supp}\mu_{S_a}.
\end{equation*}
head: environment
name: Location of the minimizer

label: eq:active-set-imag
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $G(z+i\varepsilon)=-u_\varepsilon-i\gamma_\varepsilon$ with
$\gamma_\varepsilon\succ0$.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:Dyson-scale},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:active-set-imag}
   \bigl(\mathcal C_{b_\varepsilon}-\eta\bigr)(\gamma_\varepsilon)
   =\varepsilon I
   \qquad(\varepsilon>0).
\end{equation}

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Proof of (i).}
Put $\gamma:=-\operatorname{Im}G\succeq0$, so that
$\gamma_{\varepsilon_k}\to\gamma\neq0$.  Passing to the limit in
\eqref{eq:active-set-imag} along $\varepsilon_k$ gives
$
   \bigl(\mathcal C_{b_*}-\eta\bigr)(\gamma)=0.
$
Applying $\mathcal C_{b_*^{-1/2}}$ and writing
$Q:=b_*^{1/2}\gamma\,b_*^{1/2}\neq0$, we obtain
$\widehat\eta_{b_*}(Q)=Q$.  Hence $\|\widehat\eta_{b_*}\|\geq1$.  On the
other hand, $b_*\in\mathcal F$ by
Proposition~\ref{prop:attainment-cluster-point}, so
$\|\widehat\eta_{b_*}\|\leq1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:feasible-pf}.  Thus
$\|\widehat\eta_{b_*}\|=1$, and \eqref{eq:interior-feasible} shows that
$b_*$ is not an interior point of $\mathcal F$.  If
$-\operatorname{Im}G\succ0$, then $b_\varepsilon\to b_z$ by
Proposition~\ref{prop:normalizer-limit}(i), and the first statement
applies with $b_*=b_z$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Proof of (ii).}
In a gap, $b_\varepsilon\to b_z\succ0$ by
Proposition~\ref{prop:normalizer-limit}(ii), and by
\eqref{eq:app-Y-expansion},
\begin{equation*}
   \varepsilon^{-1}\gamma_\varepsilon\longrightarrow D=-G'(z)\succ0.
\end{equation*}
Dividing \eqref{eq:active-set-imag} by $\varepsilon$ and letting
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$ gives \eqref{eq:gap-stability}.  Apply
$\mathcal C_{b_z^{-1/2}}$ and put
$Q':=b_z^{1/2}D\,b_z^{1/2}\succ0$:
\begin{equation*}
   Q'-\widehat\eta_{b_z}(Q')=b_z^{-1}.
\end{equation*}
Now argue as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:Dyson-scale}.  Choose a
nonzero $P_0\succeq0$ with $\widehat\eta_{b_z}(P_0)=rP_0$ and
$r=\|\widehat\eta_{b_z}\|$, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:feasible-pf}.
Hilbert--Schmidt self-adjointness of $\widehat\eta_{b_z}$ gives
\begin{equation*}
   (1-r)\langle P_0,Q'\rangle
   =\langle P_0,Q'\rangle-\langle\widehat\eta_{b_z}(P_0),Q'\rangle
   =\langle P_0,b_z^{-1}\rangle.
\end{equation*}
Both pairings are strictly positive, because $P_0$ is nonzero and
positive semidefinite while $Q'$ and $b_z^{-1}$ are positive definite.
Therefore $r<1$, and $b_z\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal F$ by
\eqref{eq:interior-feasible}.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{The equivalence.}
At a nondegenerate regular point either
$-\operatorname{Im}G(z+i0)\succ0$, in which case $z\in\operatorname{supp}\mu_{S_a}$
and $b_z\in\partial\mathcal F$ by (i), or $z$ lies in a gap, in which
case $b_z\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal F$ by (ii).
head: environment

label: rem:active-set
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:active-set}
Part~(i) requires only $\operatorname{Im}G(z+i0)\neq0$.  Hence at a
degenerate regular point every positive definite cluster point of the
regularized scales lies on $\partial\mathcal F$.  The identity
\eqref{eq:gap-stability} is the first-order term in $\varepsilon$ of
the imaginary Dyson equation \eqref{eq:dyson-imag-unbalanced}; in a gap
the zeroth-order term vanishes identically, and it is the derivative
$D=-G'(z)$ that certifies strict feasibility.
head: environment

label: lem:boundary-invertible
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:boundary-invertible}
Let $T$ be a self-adjoint matrix semicircle with mean $a'$ and covariance
map $\kappa$, and let $y\in\mathbb R$ be a point at which the boundary
value $G_T(y+i0)$ exists.  Then $G_T(y+i0)$ is invertible.
head: environment
name: Boundary values are invertible

title: Proof
body_md:
By the Dyson equation,
$G_T(w)^{-1}=wI-a'-\kappa\bigl(G_T(w)\bigr)$, and the right-hand side
converges as $w\to y$.  Hence $G_T(w)^{-1}$ converges, and passing to the
limit in $G_T(w)G_T(w)^{-1}=I$ shows that $G_T(y+i0)$ is invertible.
head: environment

label: rem:attainment
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:attainment}
Corollary~\ref{cor:regularized-value-limit} proves attainment
at nondegenerate regular points. More generally,
Proposition~\ref{prop:attainment-cluster-point} shows that
any positive definite cluster point of the regularized
scales is a minimizer. We explain what this criterion gives
in the different boundary regimes.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Finite boundary values.}
Suppose that the finite limit $G:=G(x+i0)$ exists.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-invertible}, $G$ is invertible.
The unitary factorization
\begin{equation*}
   G(x+i\varepsilon)
   =
   b_\varepsilon^{-1/2}
   U_\varepsilon
   b_\varepsilon^{-1/2}
\end{equation*}
therefore gives
\begin{equation*}
   \det b_\varepsilon
   =
   |\det G(x+i\varepsilon)|^{-1}
   \longrightarrow
   |\det G|^{-1}\in(0,\infty).
\end{equation*}

Consequently, an upper bound on the scales along a sequence
also gives a uniform positive lower bound on their eigenvalues.
Indeed, suppose that
$\|b_{\varepsilon_k}\|\leq M$ for some
$\varepsilon_k\downarrow0$. For all sufficiently large $k$,
we have $\det b_{\varepsilon_k}\geq d$ for some $d>0$, and hence
\begin{equation*}
   \lambda_{\min}(b_{\varepsilon_k})
   \geq
   \frac{\det b_{\varepsilon_k}}
        {\|b_{\varepsilon_k}\|^{m-1}}
   \geq
   \frac{d}{M^{m-1}}>0.
\end{equation*}
Thus these scales lie in a compact subset of the positive
definite cone. A further subsequence converges to
$b_*\succ0$, and
Proposition~\ref{prop:attainment-cluster-point} gives
\begin{equation*}
   b_*\in\mathcal F,
   \qquad
   F_x(b_*)
   =
   \inf_{b\in\mathcal F}F_x(b)
   =
   \log\Delta(S_a-x)+\frac12.
\end{equation*}

Therefore, whenever $G(x+i0)$ exists as a finite matrix,
boundedness of the regularized scales along just one sequence
is sufficient for attainment. Convergence of the whole family
is not required. We do not know whether such a bounded sequence
always exists, in particular at degenerate regular points
and spectral edges. In Example~\ref{exa:coupled}, numerical
computations suggest convergence of the normalizers.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Singular boundary values.}
If $G(x+i0)$ does not exist as a finite matrix, the Puiseux
expansion in Lemma~\ref{lem:local-puiseux-control} gives
$
   \|G(x+i\varepsilon)\|\longrightarrow\infty.
$
The unitary factorization implies
\begin{equation*}
   \|G(x+i\varepsilon)\|
   \leq
   \|b_\varepsilon^{-1}\|,
\end{equation*}
and therefore
\begin{equation*}
   \lambda_{\min}(b_\varepsilon)
   =
   \|b_\varepsilon^{-1}\|^{-1}
   \leq
   \|G(x+i\varepsilon)\|^{-1}
   \longrightarrow0.
\end{equation*}
Thus the regularized scales leave every compact subset of the
positive definite cone, and the cluster-point criterion does
not apply. This escape does not by itself rule out attainment
by some other feasible matrix: the criterion is sufficient,
not an established characterization of attainment.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Non-attainment.}
At an atom, the infimum is $-\infty$ and cannot be attained,
because every $b\in\mathcal F$ satisfies
\begin{equation*}
   F_x(b)
   \geq
   \operatorname{tr}_m\log b
   >
   -\infty.
\end{equation*}
At general non-atomic singular points, the preceding
compactness argument leaves attainment unresolved.

The centered case provides a more precise conclusion.
For $a=0$ and $x=0$,
Theorem~\ref{thm:centered-capacity} states that the infimum
is attained if and only if $\eta$ is symmetrically
doubly-stochastic scalable. In particular, when
$\operatorname{Cap}(\eta)>0$ but $\eta$ is not symmetrically
doubly-stochastic scalable, the infimum is finite but is
not attained.
head: environment
name: Attainment and the behavior of the regularized scales

label: exa:coupled
title: Example
body_md:
\label{exa:coupled}
Let $m=2$, $r=1$, $A_1=E_{11}$ and
$a=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&c\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with $c\neq0$,
so that
\[
   S_a=\begin{pmatrix}s&c\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The covariance pencil is reducible, but the mean couples the two
coordinates.  All entries commute, so
$S_a=\lambda_+(s)P_+(s)+\lambda_-(s)P_-(s)$ with
$\lambda_\pm(t)=\tfrac12\bigl(t+d\pm\sqrt{(t-d)^2+4c^2}\bigr)$ and rank-one
spectral projections $P_\pm(t)$.  Since $\lambda_\pm'>0$ and
$\lambda_+>d>\lambda_-$, the density of the matrix-valued spectral measure
at $x=\lambda_\pm(t)$ is
$P_\pm(t)\,\rho_{\mathrm{sc}}(t)/\lambda_\pm'(t)$.  It is bounded and has
rank exactly one at every interior point of the support
$\lambda_+([-2,2])\cup\lambda_-([-2,2])$.  Hence every interior point of
the support is a degenerate regular point, and none of them is a limit of
nondegenerate regular points.  By Theorem~\ref{thm:real-axis} the
variational formula nevertheless holds there, with
\[
   \log\Delta(S_a-x)
   =
   \tfrac12\int_{-2}^2\log\bigl|(t-x)(d-x)-c^2\bigr|\,d\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}(t).
\]
head: environment
name: Degenerate points filling the support

label: cor:brown
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:brown}
Let $a_0,a_1,\dots,a_r\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ be arbitrary matrices and
\[
   S:=a_0\otimes1+\sum_{i=1}^ra_i\otimes s_i .
\]
For $z\in\mathbb C$ put
\[
   A_0(z):=\begin{pmatrix}0&a_0-zI\\ a_0^*-\overline{z}I&0\end{pmatrix},
   \qquad
   A_i:=\begin{pmatrix}0&a_i\\ a_i^*&0\end{pmatrix}
   \quad(i=1,\dots,r),
\]
all Hermitian in $M_{2m}(\mathbb C)$, and let
$\eta^{\mathrm h}(B):=\sum_iA_iBA_i$, $L^{\mathrm h}_b:=\mathcal C_b+\eta^{\mathrm h}$,
\begin{align*}
   \mathcal{F}^{\mathrm h}&:=\{b\succ0:\ \mathcal C_b-\eta^{\mathrm h}\succeq0\}
   \subset M_{2m}(\mathbb C), 
   \\
   F^{\mathrm h}_z(b)
   &:=
   \operatorname{tr}_{2m}\log b
   +
   \sup_{u=u^*}
   \Bigl\{
      \left\langle A_0(z),u\right\rangle-\frac12\left\langle u,L^{\mathrm h}_bu\right\rangle
   \Bigr\}.
\end{align*}
Then, for every $z\in\mathbb C$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:brown-variational}
   \log\Delta(S-z)
   =
   -\frac12+\inf_{b\in\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm h}}F^{\mathrm h}_z(b)
   \qquad\text{in }[-\infty,\infty),
\end{equation}
and both sides equal $-\infty$ if and only if $S-z$ has a nontrivial
kernel.  If $S-z$ is invertible, the infimum is attained.  Consequently the
Brown measure of $S$ is the distributional Laplacian
$\frac1{2\pi}\nabla_z^2$ of the right-hand side of
\eqref{eq:brown-variational}.
head: environment
name: Brown measure of matrix-valued semicircular elements

title: Proof
body_md:
Let
\[
   H_z
   :=
   \begin{pmatrix}0&S-z\\ S^*-\overline{z}&0\end{pmatrix}
   =
   A_0(z)\otimes1+\sum_{i=1}^rA_i\otimes s_i
   \in M_{2m}(\mathbb C)\otimes\mathcal A .
\]
This is a self-adjoint matrix semicircle with Hermitian mean $A_0(z)$ and
Hermitian Kraus operators $A_i$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:real-axis} applies
to it at the real point $x=0$.  Its feasible set and functional are
$\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm h}$ and $F^{\mathrm h}_z$, because the shift $A_0(z)-0\cdot I$
is $A_0(z)$.  Since $S^*-\overline{z}=(S-z)^*$, the properties of the
Fuglede--Kadison determinant \cite{FugledeKadison1952} give
$\Delta(H_z)=\Delta(S-z)^{1/2}\Delta((S-z)^*)^{1/2}=\Delta(S-z)$; see
\cite[Lemma~3.5(ii)]{MaiSpeicher2024}.  This proves
\eqref{eq:brown-variational}.

By Corollary~\ref{cor:minus-infinity-atoms}, both sides are $-\infty$ exactly when
$\mu_{H_z}$ has an atom at $0$, that is, when $H_z$ has a nontrivial
kernel.  Since $\ker H_z=\ker(S-z)\oplus\ker((S-z)^*)$ and, in a finite
von Neumann algebra, $\ker T$ and $\ker T^*$ have the same trace, this
happens if and only if $\ker(S-z)\neq\{0\}$.

If $S-z$ is invertible, then $H_z$ is invertible, so $0$ lies in an open
component of $\mathbb R\setminus\operatorname{supp}\mu_{H_z}$ and is a nondegenerate
regular point of $H_z$; the infimum is attained by Corollary~\ref{cor:regularized-value-limit}.
Finally, $z\mapsto\log\Delta(S-z)$ is the logarithmic potential of the
Brown measure of $S$, which is recovered from it as
$\frac1{2\pi}\nabla_z^2\log\Delta(S-z)$ in the sense of distributions
\cite{Brown1986}.
head: environment

label: lem:ds-capacity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:ds-capacity}
Let $\Phi:M_m(\mathbb C)\to M_m(\mathbb C)$ be completely positive,
unital, and trace-preserving.  Then
$
   \operatorname{Cap}(\Phi)=1.
$
head: environment
name: Capacity of a doubly stochastic map

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\Phi(I)=I$, the competitor $X=I$ gives
$
   \operatorname{Cap}(\Phi)\leq1.
$

Conversely, let $X\succ0$ with $\det X=1$.  Since $\log$ is operator
concave and $\Phi$ is unital and completely positive, the operator Jensen
inequality \cite{HansenPedersen1982} gives
\[
   \log\Phi(X)
   \succeq
   \Phi(\log X).
\]
Taking normalized traces and using trace preservation,
\[
   \operatorname{tr}_m\log\Phi(X)
   \geq
   \operatorname{tr}_m\Phi(\log X)
   =
   \operatorname{tr}_m\log X
   =
   0.
\]
Hence
$
   \det\Phi(X)\geq1.
$
Taking the infimum over all $X\succ0$ with $\det X=1$ gives
$
   \operatorname{Cap}(\Phi)\geq1.
$
head: environment

label: thm:centered-capacity
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Centered variational problem and capacity

label: eq:capacity-scaled-b
title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove the lower bound.

Let $b\in\mathcal{F}$.  Recall
$
   \widehat\eta_b
   =
   \mathcal C_{b^{-1/2}}
   \eta
   \mathcal C_{b^{-1/2}}
   =
   \mathcal S_{b^{-1/2},b^{-1/2}}(\eta).
$
By the scaling rule \eqref{eq:capacity-scaling},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:capacity-scaled-b}
   \operatorname{Cap}(\widehat\eta_b)
   =
   \det(b)^{-2}
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta).
\end{equation}

Taking $X=I$ in the definition of capacity gives
$
   \operatorname{Cap}(\widehat\eta_b)
   \leq
   \det\widehat\eta_b(I).
$
Since $b\in\mathcal{F}$, Lemma~\ref{lem:feasible-pf} gives
$
   I-\widehat\eta_b\succeq0
$
as an operator on Hilbert--Schmidt space.  Pairing this inequality with
$I$ yields
\[
   \operatorname{tr}_m\widehat\eta_b(I)
   =
   \left\langle I,\widehat\eta_b(I)\right\rangle
   \leq
   \left\langle I,I\right\rangle
   =
   1.
\]
Moreover, $\widehat\eta_b(I)\succeq0$ as a matrix.  Hence the
arithmetic--geometric mean inequality gives
\[
   \det\widehat\eta_b(I)
   \leq
   \bigl(
      \operatorname{tr}_m\widehat\eta_b(I)
   \bigr)^m
   \leq1.
\]
Therefore
$
   \operatorname{Cap}(\widehat\eta_b)\leq1.
$
Using \eqref{eq:capacity-scaled-b},
$
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta)
   \leq
   \det(b)^2.
$
Since
$
   \Delta(b)=\det(b)^{1/m},
$
we obtain
\[
   \Delta(b)
   \geq
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta)^{1/(2m)}.
\]
Taking the infimum over $b\in\mathcal{F}$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:capacity-lower}
   \inf_{b\in\mathcal{F}}\Delta(b)
   \geq
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta)^{1/(2m)}.
\end{equation}

We next prove the reverse inequality.

Suppose first that $\eta$ is symmetrically doubly-stochastic scalable.
Choose $C\succ0$ satisfying
$
   \eta(C)=C^{-1}
$
and put
$
   b:=C^{-1}.
$
Then
$
   \widehat\eta_b
   =
   \mathcal S_{C^{1/2},C^{1/2}}(\eta)
$
is unital:
\[
   \widehat\eta_b(I)
   =
   C^{1/2}\eta(C)C^{1/2}
   =
   I.
\]
The map $\widehat\eta_b$ is Hilbert--Schmidt self-adjoint, so unitality
also implies trace preservation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
   \operatorname{tr}_m\widehat\eta_b(X)
   &=
   \left\langle I,\widehat\eta_b(X)\right\rangle\\
   &=
   \left\langle \widehat\eta_b(I),X\right\rangle\\
   &=
   \operatorname{tr}_m X.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus $\widehat\eta_b$ is doubly stochastic.

By the Kadison--Schwarz inequality,
\[
   \widehat\eta_b(X)^*
   \widehat\eta_b(X)
   \preceq
   \widehat\eta_b(X^*X).
\]
Taking normalized traces and using trace preservation,
$
   \|\widehat\eta_b(X)\|_2^2
   \leq
   \|X\|_2^2.
$
Hence
$
   \|\widehat\eta_b\|_{\mathrm{HS}\to\mathrm{HS}}\leq1,
$
and therefore $b\in\mathcal{F}$.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:ds-capacity},
$
   \operatorname{Cap}(\widehat\eta_b)=1.
$
Using \eqref{eq:capacity-scaled-b},
$
   1
   =
   \det(b)^{-2}\operatorname{Cap}(\eta),
$
so
$
   \det(b)^2
   =
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta).
$
Consequently,
\[
   \Delta(b)
   =
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta)^{1/(2m)}.
\]
Thus equality holds in \eqref{eq:capacity-lower} whenever an exact
symmetric doubly-stochastic scaling exists.

For a general $\eta$, introduce the strictly positive regularization
\begin{equation}\label{eq:capacity-regularization}
   \eta_\varepsilon(X)
   :=
   \eta(X)
   +
   \varepsilon\,\operatorname{tr}_m(X)I,
   \qquad
   \varepsilon>0.
\end{equation}
Each $\eta_\varepsilon$ is self-adjoint, completely positive, and strictly
positive; hence it is symmetrically doubly-stochastic scalable, \cite{KarginNonSingular2026}.  Denote its
feasible set by
\[
   \mathcal{F}_\varepsilon
   :=
   \left\{
      b\succ0:
      \mathcal C_b-\eta_\varepsilon\succeq0
   \right\}.
\]
Since
$
   \eta_\varepsilon\succeq\eta,
$
we have
$
   \mathcal{F}_\varepsilon\subseteq\mathcal{F}.
$
By the already proved scalable case,
\[
   \inf_{b\in\mathcal{F}_\varepsilon}\Delta(b)
   =
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta_\varepsilon)^{1/(2m)}.
\]
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:capacity-upper-eps}
   \inf_{b\in\mathcal{F}}\Delta(b)
   \leq
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta_\varepsilon)^{1/(2m)}.
\end{equation}

It remains to let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$.  We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:capacity-continuity}
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta_\varepsilon)
   \longrightarrow
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta).
\end{equation}
Since
$
   \eta_\varepsilon(X)\succeq\eta(X),$ with$X\succ0$,
monotonicity of the determinant on the positive cone gives
$
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta_\varepsilon)
   \geq
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta).
$

Conversely, fix $\delta>0$ and choose $X_\delta\succ0$ with
$
   \det X_\delta=1
$
and
\[
   \det\eta(X_\delta)
   \leq
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta)+\delta.
\]
For this fixed $X_\delta$,
$
   \eta_\varepsilon(X_\delta)
   \longrightarrow
   \eta(X_\delta),
$
so
$
   \det\eta_\varepsilon(X_\delta)
   \longrightarrow
   \det\eta(X_\delta).
$
Since
\[
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta_\varepsilon)
   \leq
   \det\eta_\varepsilon(X_\delta),
\]
we obtain
\[
   \limsup_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta_\varepsilon)
   \leq
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta)+\delta.
\]
Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ proves
\eqref{eq:capacity-continuity}.

Passing to the limit in
\eqref{eq:capacity-upper-eps} gives
\[
   \inf_{b\in\mathcal{F}}\Delta(b)
   \leq
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta)^{1/(2m)}.
\]
Together with \eqref{eq:capacity-lower}, this proves
\eqref{eq:centered-capacity}.

It remains to characterize attainment.  Suppose that
$b\in\mathcal{F}$ attains the infimum.  Then
$
   \det(b)^2
   =
   \operatorname{Cap}(\eta),
$
and therefore, by \eqref{eq:capacity-scaled-b},
$
   \operatorname{Cap}(\widehat\eta_b)=1.
$
In the chain
\[
   \operatorname{Cap}(\widehat\eta_b)
   \leq
   \det\widehat\eta_b(I)
   \leq
   \bigl(
      \operatorname{tr}_m\widehat\eta_b(I)
   \bigr)^m
   \leq
   1,
\]
all inequalities must be equalities.  In particular,
$
   \operatorname{tr}_m\widehat\eta_b(I)=1
$
and
$
   \det\widehat\eta_b(I)=1.
$
Equality in the arithmetic--geometric mean inequality forces
$
   \widehat\eta_b(I)=I.
$
Since $\widehat\eta_b$ is self-adjoint, it is therefore doubly stochastic.

Writing
$
   C:=b^{-1},
$
the identity
$
   \widehat\eta_b(I)=I
$
is exactly
$
   C^{1/2}\eta(C)C^{1/2}=I,
$
or
$
   \eta(C)=C^{-1}.
$
Thus $\eta$ is symmetrically doubly-stochastic scalable.

The converse was proved above: every symmetric doubly-stochastic scaler
produces an optimizer.

title: Corollary

name: Mai--Speicher formula

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:centered-F},
\[
   \inf_{b\in\mathcal{F}}F_0(b)
   =
   \inf_{b\in\mathcal{F}}\log\Delta(b).
\]
Theorem~\ref{thm:centered-capacity} gives
\[
   \inf_{b\in\mathcal{F}}\log\Delta(b)
   =
   \frac1{2m}
   \log\operatorname{Cap}(\eta).
\]
Substituting this into Theorem~\ref{thm:real-axis}, applied with
$a=0$ at the point $x=0$, gives
\eqref{eq:mai-speicher}.

label: rem:capacity-attainment
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:capacity-attainment}
The theorem separates two qualitatively different centered regimes.

If $\eta$ is symmetrically doubly-stochastic scalable, the capacity
minimum is realized by a finite positive scale.

If $\operatorname{Cap}(\eta)>0$ but $\eta$ is not symmetrically
doubly-stochastic scalable, then
\[
   \inf_{b\in\mathcal{F}}\Delta(b)>0
\]
but the infimum is not attained.  Any minimizing sequence must therefore
leave every compact subset of the positive definite cone; otherwise a
convergent subsequence would produce an optimizer.

Thus non-attainment of the centered variational problem is precisely the
failure of exact symmetric doubly-stochastic scaling.

title: Proof
body_md:
We treat the two cases separately.

\smallskip

\noindent
\textbf{Case 1: strictly negative imaginary part.}
Assume
$
   Y:=-\operatorname{Im}G\succ0.
$
Then
\[
   X_\varepsilon\longrightarrow
   X:=\operatorname{Re}G,
   \qquad
   Y_\varepsilon\longrightarrow Y.
\]
Since $Y\succ0$, the maps
$
   Y\longmapsto Y^{\pm1/2}
$
are continuous in a neighborhood of $Y$.  Hence every factor in
\eqref{eq:app-pup-normalizer} converges, and therefore
\[
   b_\varepsilon^{-1}
   \longrightarrow
   Y^{1/2}
   \left(
      I+
      \bigl(
         Y^{-1/2}XY^{-1/2}
      \bigr)^2
   \right)^{1/2}
   Y^{1/2}.
\]
The right-hand side is precisely the inverse of the unitary normalizer
obtained by applying Lemma~\ref{lem:pup} directly to $G$.  This proves
part~(i).

\smallskip

\noindent
\textbf{Case 2: a real resolvent gap.}
Suppose now that $z$ belongs to an open component of
$\mathbb R\setminus\operatorname{supp}\mu_{S_a}$.  Then the operator-valued Cauchy
transform extends analytically across a neighborhood of $z$, and
$
   G(z)=G(z)^*.
$
Moreover,
\[
   G'(z)
   =
   -
   \int_{\mathbb R}
   \frac{1}{(z-t)^2}\,dv(t),
\]
where $v$ is the $M_m(\mathbb C)$-valued spectral measure of $S_a$.
Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:app-D}
   D:=-G'(z)
   =
   \int_{\mathbb R}
   \frac{1}{(z-t)^2}\,dv(t)
   \succ0.
\end{equation}
Indeed, for every nonzero vector $\xi$,
\[
   \langle\xi,D\xi\rangle
   =
   \int_{\mathbb R}
   \frac{1}{(z-t)^2}\,
   d\langle\xi,v(t)\xi\rangle
   >0.
\]

By Schwarz reflection,
$
   G(\overline{w})=G(w)^*,
$
so the Taylor expansion of $G(z+i\varepsilon)$ at $z$ has the form
\begin{align}
   X_\varepsilon
   &=
   G(z)+O(\varepsilon^2),
   \label{eq:app-X-expansion}\\
   Y_\varepsilon
   &=
   \varepsilon D+O(\varepsilon^3).
   \label{eq:app-Y-expansion}
\end{align}
It is convenient to write
$
   D_\varepsilon
   :=
   \varepsilon^{-1}Y_\varepsilon.
$
Then
$
   D_\varepsilon\longrightarrow D\succ0.
$

Define
\[
   T_\varepsilon
   :=
   D_\varepsilon^{-1/2}
   X_\varepsilon
   D_\varepsilon^{-1/2}.
\]
Since
$
   Y_\varepsilon
   =
   \varepsilon D_\varepsilon,
$
we have
\[
   Y_\varepsilon^{-1/2}
   X_\varepsilon
   Y_\varepsilon^{-1/2}
   =
   \varepsilon^{-1}T_\varepsilon.
\]
Substituting this into \eqref{eq:app-pup-normalizer},
\begin{align*}
   b_\varepsilon^{-1}
   &=
   \varepsilon^{1/2}D_\varepsilon^{1/2}
   \left(
      I+\varepsilon^{-2}T_\varepsilon^2
   \right)^{1/2}
   \varepsilon^{1/2}D_\varepsilon^{1/2}\\
   &=
   D_\varepsilon^{1/2}
   \left(
      \varepsilon^2I+T_\varepsilon^2
   \right)^{1/2}
   D_\varepsilon^{1/2}.
\end{align*}
Now
\[
   T_\varepsilon
   \longrightarrow
   T
   :=
   D^{-1/2}G(z)D^{-1/2}.
\]
Since $G(z)$ is invertible, so is $T$.  Therefore, by continuity of the
functional calculus,
$
   \left(
      \varepsilon^2I+T_\varepsilon^2
   \right)^{1/2}
   \longrightarrow
   |T|.
$
Consequently,
\[
   b_\varepsilon^{-1}
   \longrightarrow
   D^{1/2}|T|D^{1/2},
\]
which is exactly \eqref{eq:gap-normalizer}.

It remains to verify that the limiting matrix is indeed a unitary
normalizer of $G(z)$.  Since $T=T^*$ is invertible,
\[
   T
   =
   |T|^{1/2}
   J
   |T|^{1/2},
   \qquad
   J:=\operatorname{sign}(T),
\]
where $J=J^*$ and $J^2=I$.  Put
$
   L
   :=
   D^{1/2}|T|^{1/2}.
$
Then
\[
   G(z)
   =
   D^{1/2}TD^{1/2}
   =
   LJL^*,
\]
and
\[
   LL^*
   =
   D^{1/2}|T|D^{1/2}
   =
   b_z^{-1}.
\]
Take the polar decomposition
  $
   L=b_z^{-1/2}V,$
   where $
   V\in U(m).$
It follows that
\[
   G(z)
   =
   b_z^{-1/2}
   (VJV^*)
   b_z^{-1/2}.
\]
Since $VJV^*$ is unitary,
\[
   b_z^{1/2}G(z)b_z^{1/2}
   =
   VJV^*
\]
is unitary.  Thus $b_z$ is a unitary normalizer of $G(z)$.

Finally, if $G(z)$ is definite, then $T$ is definite as well.  Hence
$
   |T|
   =
   \pm T,
$
with the sign chosen according to the sign of $G(z)$.  Therefore
\[
   b_z^{-1}
   =
   D^{1/2}|T|D^{1/2}
   =
   \pm G(z)
   =
   |G(z)|,
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:definite-normalizer}.

title: Remark
body_md:
The appearance of
\[
   D=-G'(z)
\]
in \eqref{eq:gap-normalizer} reflects the fact that when the boundary
value $G(z)$ is self-adjoint and indefinite, it may admit more than one
positive unitary normalizer.  The vertical regularization
$G(z+i\varepsilon)$ selects a canonical one, and this selection depends on
the first transverse derivative of the Cauchy transform at the real axis.

When $G(z)$ is definite, the ambiguity disappears and the selected
normalizer reduces to the familiar expression
$
   |G(z)|^{-1}.
$

label: lem:local-puiseux-control
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:local-puiseux-control}
Fix $x\in\mathbb R$.  There exist an integer $N\geq1$, a radius $r>0$,
matrices $C_k\in M_m(\mathbb C)$, and an integer $k_0$ with
$C_{k_0}\neq0$ such that the branch of $G$ selected from the upper
half-plane has a convergent Puiseux expansion
\begin{equation}\label{eq:local-puiseux}
   G(x+\zeta)
   =
   \sum_{k\geq k_0}
   C_k\zeta^{k/N},
   \qquad
   0<|\zeta|<r,
   \quad
   0<\arg\zeta<\pi.
\end{equation}
Here the fractional powers are taken with the branch determined by
$0<\arg\zeta<\pi$.

Set
$
   \theta(x):=-\frac{k_0}{N}.
$
Then
$
   0\leq\theta(x)\leq 1
 $
and, after decreasing $r$ if necessary,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:local-G-bound}
   \|G(x+\zeta)\|
   \leq
   C|\zeta|^{-\theta(x)}
\end{equation}
throughout the upper half-disc
$
   0<|\zeta|<r,$
   $
   \operatorname{Im}\zeta>0.
$
head: environment
name: Local Puiseux control

title: Proof
body_md:
By entrywise algebraicity, the classical Newton--Puiseux theorem \cite{Walker1950} gives a
convergent Puiseux expansion for every entry $G_{pq}$ on the local branch
selected from $\mathbb C^+$.  Taking a common multiple of the finitely
many ramification indices gives \eqref{eq:local-puiseux}.

Factoring out the lowest nonzero power gives
\[
   G(x+\zeta)
   =
   \zeta^{-\theta(x)}
   \left(
      C_{k_0}
      +
      \sum_{k>k_0}
      C_k\zeta^{(k-k_0)/N}
   \right).
\]
The series in parentheses is uniformly bounded for sufficiently small
$\zeta$ in the upper half-disc.  This gives
\eqref{eq:local-G-bound}.

It remains to prove  that  $0\leq\theta(x)\leq 1$.  The resolvent estimate gives
$
   \|G(x+i\varepsilon)\|
   \leq
   \frac1{\varepsilon}.
$
Comparison with the leading Puiseux behavior shows that
$
   \theta(x)\leq1.
$

Suppose, on the other hand, that $\theta(x)<0$.  Then
$
   G(x+i\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.
$
The Dyson equation gives
\[
   G(w)^{-1}
   =
   wI-a-\eta(G(w)).
\]
Its right-hand side remains bounded as $w\to x$, whereas
$\|G(w)\|\to0$ would imply
$
   \|G(w)^{-1}\|\longrightarrow\infty.
$
This contradiction proves $\theta(x)\geq0$.

label: lem:theta-one-atom
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Atoms and the exponent one

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $\theta(x)=1$.  The Puiseux expansion gives
$
   i\varepsilon G(x+i\varepsilon)
   \longrightarrow
   P
$
for some nonzero matrix $P$.

On the other hand, by the spectral theorem,
\[
   i\varepsilon
   (x+i\varepsilon-S_a)^{-1}
   \longrightarrow
   \mathbf 1_{\{x\}}(S_a)
\]
strongly as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$.  Since the operators on the left
are uniformly bounded, applying $\mathrm{id}\otimes\tau$ gives
\[
   i\varepsilon G(x+i\varepsilon)
   \longrightarrow
   P_x
   :=
   (\mathrm{id}\otimes\tau)
   \bigl[\mathbf 1_{\{x\}}(S_a)\bigr].
\]
Hence
\[
   P=P_x\neq0.
\]
The matrix $P_x$ is positive semidefinite, so
$
   \mu_{S_a}(\{x\})
   =
   \operatorname{tr}_m P_x
   >0.
$

Conversely, suppose
$
   p:=\mu_{S_a}(\{x\})>0.
$
Since
\[
   -\operatorname{Im}g(x+i\varepsilon)
   =
   \int_{\mathbb R}
   \frac{\varepsilon}
        {(t-x)^2+\varepsilon^2}
   \,d\mu_{S_a}(t),
\]
the atom at $x$ gives
\[
   -\operatorname{Im}g(x+i\varepsilon)
   \geq
   \frac{p}{\varepsilon}.
\]
Because the normalized trace is dominated by the operator norm,
\[
   \|G(x+i\varepsilon)\|
   \geq
   \frac{p}{\varepsilon}.
\]
Together with the resolvent bound
$
   \|G(x+i\varepsilon)\|
   \leq
   \frac1{\varepsilon},
$
this forces the leading Puiseux exponent to be
$
   \theta(x)=1.
$

label: thm:nonatomic-local-regularity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:nonatomic-local-regularity}
Let $x\in\mathbb R$ satisfy
$
   \mu_{S_a}(\{x\})=0.
$
Then there exist an open interval $I\ni x$, a number $p>1$, and a
nonnegative function
$
   \rho\in L^p(I)
$
such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:local-ac}
   d\mu_{S_a}(t)\big|_I
   =
   \rho(t)\,dt.
\end{equation}

More precisely, if $\theta=\theta(x)$ is the exponent from
Lemma~\ref{lem:local-puiseux-control}, then $\theta<1$ and one may choose
$I$ so that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rho-pointwise-bound}
   0\leq
   \rho(t)
   \leq
   C|t-x|^{-\theta}
   \qquad
   \text{for a.e. }t\in I.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\[
   \rho\in L^p(I)
   \qquad
   \text{for every }
   1<p<\frac1\theta
\]
when $\theta>0$, while for $\theta=0$ one has
$
   \rho\in L^\infty(I).
$
head: environment
name: Local regularity at non-atomic points

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:theta-one-atom}, non-atomicity implies
$
   \theta:=\theta(x)<1.
$
Choose $I\ni x$ sufficiently small that the estimate
\[
   \|G(t+i\varepsilon)\|
   \leq
   C
   \bigl(
      (t-x)^2+\varepsilon^2
   \bigr)^{-\theta/2}
\]
holds for $t\in I$ and all sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$.

Define the Poisson regularization of the spectral measure by
\[
   \rho_\varepsilon(t)
   :=
   -\frac1\pi
   \operatorname{Im}g(t+i\varepsilon).
\]
Since $g$ is the scalar Cauchy transform of $\mu_{S_a}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:poisson-density}
   \rho_\varepsilon(t)
   =
   \int_{\mathbb R}
   P_\varepsilon(t-s)\,d\mu_{S_a}(s),
\end{equation}
where
\[
   P_\varepsilon(s)
   :=
   \frac1\pi
   \frac{\varepsilon}{s^2+\varepsilon^2}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
   0\leq
   \rho_\varepsilon(t)
   \leq
   \frac1\pi\|G(t+i\varepsilon)\|.
\]
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:poisson-domination}
   0\leq
   \rho_\varepsilon(t)
   \leq
   C'
   \bigl(
      (t-x)^2+\varepsilon^2
   \bigr)^{-\theta/2}
   \leq
   C'|t-x|^{-\theta}
\end{equation}
for $t\neq x$.

Let $\varphi\in C_c(I)$ be nonnegative.  From
\eqref{eq:poisson-density} and Fubini's theorem,
\[
\begin{aligned}
   \int_I
   \varphi(t)\rho_\varepsilon(t)\,dt
   &=
   \int_{\mathbb R}
   (P_\varepsilon*\varphi)(s)\,
   d\mu_{S_a}(s).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since
$
   P_\varepsilon*\varphi
   \longrightarrow
   \varphi
$
uniformly as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, we obtain
\[
   \int_I\varphi(t)\,d\mu_{S_a}(t)
   =
   \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}
   \int_I
   \varphi(t)\rho_\varepsilon(t)\,dt.
\]
Using \eqref{eq:poisson-domination},
\[
   \int_I\varphi(t)\,d\mu_{S_a}(t)
   \leq
   C'
   \int_I
   \varphi(t)|t-x|^{-\theta}\,dt.
\]
Therefore, as measures on $I$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:measure-domination}
   \mu_{S_a}|_I
   \leq
   C'|t-x|^{-\theta}\,dt.
\end{equation}
It follows that
\[
   \mu_{S_a}|_I=\rho(t)\,dt
\]
for some measurable $\rho\geq0$ satisfying
\eqref{eq:rho-pointwise-bound}.

If $\theta=0$, this immediately gives
$
   \rho\in L^\infty(I).
$
If $0<\theta<1$, then
\[
   |t-x|^{-p\theta}\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}
\]
whenever
\[
   p\theta<1.
\]
Thus
\[
   \rho\in L^p(I)
   \qquad
   \text{for every }
   1<p<\frac1\theta.
\]
Since $\theta<1$, such a $p>1$ always exists.
